title: Organic matter and compost
teaches: How organic matter improves soil structure, balancing browns and greens in a compost heap, and the breakdown of dead plants into humus

blocks.text: Gardeners recommend adding compost to fix almost every problem, whether you are dealing with heavy clay, dry sand, or struggling tomatoes. Although that advice can sound like a cure-all, it is grounded in physics and biology. Even when [[organic matter|organic]] makes up just a few percent of a soil, it shapes how the whole bed holds water, breathes, and feeds roots.

Chemical fertilizers supply dissolved salts directly to plant roots, whereas organic matter feeds the soil food web introduced in Lesson 3. Everything in the soil that cannot live on root sugars relies on dead organic material. As microbes and worms digest it over months and years, they gradually release the nitrogen, phosphorus, and sulfur locked inside the old plant tissues. The tough material left behind after this feast becomes dark, crumbly **humus**,[^humus] which soaks up water like a sponge and holds onto nutrients just as clay does. While breaking down plant matter, microbes also produce the sticky gums that glue mineral grains into the crumbs covered in the next lesson.

blocks.text: Because just a small percentage of organic matter opens up drainage channels in heavy clay while helping sandy soil hold onto moisture, adding compost improves both extremes. You can see this effect in the pores diagram from Lesson 2, where raising the organic matter slider improved water and air balance across every soil texture.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Mineral fertilizer feeds plants directly, whereas [[organic matter|organic]] feeds the soil life that supports plants.
Organic matter releases nutrients gradually, holds water, and supplies the glue that binds soil into crumbs.

blocks.text: Compost microbes need carbon to burn for energy and nitrogen to build proteins. Their ideal diet contains roughly twenty-five to thirty parts carbon for every one part nitrogen.[^cn] Dry, tough materials like autumn leaves, straw, and cardboard are rich in carbon, so gardeners call them **browns**. Fresh, juicy materials like grass clippings and kitchen scraps contain much more nitrogen and are known as **greens**. A compost heap breaks down smoothly when your mix of browns and greens matches what the microbes need.

blocks.caption: A compost bin, built one bucket at a time
blocks.task: Build a heap of at least three buckets with a carbon-to-nitrogen ratio between 20 and 40

blocks.text: When a heap has too many greens, the microbes cannot use all the nitrogen, and the excess escapes as smelly ammonia gas while the pile slumps into an airless, slimy mat. When a heap has too many browns, the microbes run short of nitrogen and decay slows to a crawl. If you balance the mix, keep it as damp as a wrung-out sponge, and turn it occasionally to let air in, a pile a metre across will heat up to 55 °C or higher and turn into finished compost in a few months.[^heat]

That same carbon-to-nitrogen math applies right in the garden bed. If you dig fresh wood chips or sawdust into the soil, the microbes trying to digest all that carbon will pull dissolved nitrogen out of the surrounding soil to balance their diet, leaving your crops short of nitrogen for several weeks.[^robbery] Spread on the surface as mulch, however, fresh wood chips cause no trouble because microbes can only nibble at the thin layer where the wood touches the damp soil.

Once a bucket of dead leaves enters the soil, different compounds break down at very different speeds. Microbes consume the simple sugars and proteins within a few weeks. Cellulose, the main structural fiber in plant cell walls, takes several months to break down, while lignin, the tough compound that makes bark and stems woody, takes years. Soil organisms breathe out most of the carbon from each meal as carbon dioxide (CO₂), leaving only a small fraction behind as stable humus.

blocks.text: Within a couple of years, soil life consumes most of the compost you add. This disappearance is a sign of a healthy bed, since the process of eating organic matter is what powers the food web and releases plant nutrients. Because the web steadily burns through its fuel supply, you need to top up a garden bed with fresh organic matter every year to keep it fertile.[^model] Lesson 8 covers simple ways to keep organic matter cycling through the seasons.

blocks.title: Using compost and manure
points: Spread 2 to 5 cm of compost onto the surface of each bed once a year, in autumn or spring. Leave it on top rather than digging it in, as earthworms will pull it down for you.
Finished compost looks dark and crumbly and smells like damp woodland earth, with very few recognizable plant scraps left. Sieve out any chunky woody bits and toss them into your next heap.

Always let animal manure rot for at least six months before putting it on a food bed, since fresh manure can burn tender roots, sprout weed seeds, and carry harmful bacteria onto salad crops. Check where bought manure came from to avoid herbicide contamination,[^herbicide] and never put cat or dog droppings in garden compost.

Keep meat, fish, and dairy out of an open heap so you do not attract rats. Unless your pile reliably heats up above 55 °C, leave out diseased plants, weeds that have gone to seed, and the creeping roots of perennial weeds like bindweed and couch grass.

blocks.title: Try it in the garden
points: Start a compost heap, or check on the one you have. If it smells like ammonia, mix in dry browns and turn it to add air. If it looks dry and dusty, water it with a hose; if it feels soggy, stir in dry leaves or shredded cardboard. Push your hand into the middle of the pile to feel if the microbes are generating heat.

Rake up fallen autumn leaves and stash them in burlap sacks or a wire cage next to your bin. Stockpiling leaves in autumn gives you a ready supply of browns to balance out the rush of green grass clippings and kitchen scraps the following summer.

blocks.caption: Quiz on organic matter and compost

items.question: Why does adding compost improve both heavy clay and dry, sandy soil?
options: It opens up drainage channels in clay and helps sand hold water
It changes the mineral grains of both into silt
It actually only helps clay soils
items.why: Organic matter glues clay into crumbs with large pores between them, while adding spongy, water-holding material to sand.

items.question: A pile of fresh grass clippings smells strongly of ammonia. What does it need?
options: Dry browns, such as autumn leaves or straw, mixed in for air and carbon
More fresh grass clippings
A tight plastic cover to hold the smell in
items.why: Fresh grass has about 15 parts carbon to 1 part nitrogen, and mats down tightly. Mixing in dry browns supplies carbon and opens air spaces.

items.question: Roughly what carbon-to-nitrogen ratio do compost microbes need in their diet?
options: 25 to 30 parts carbon to 1 part nitrogen
1 part carbon to 1 part nitrogen
300 parts carbon to 1 part nitrogen
The ratio does not affect decay
items.why: Microbes work fastest around 25 to 30 parts carbon to 1 part nitrogen. Much lower loses nitrogen as ammonia; much higher slows decay down.

items.question: If you dig fresh sawdust into a vegetable bed before planting, what happens over the next few weeks?
options: The crops struggle because microbes pull nitrogen from the soil
The crops grow much faster from the extra carbon
Nothing changes for the plants
items.why: Sawdust is almost pure carbon, so microbes absorb soil nitrogen to digest it. Kept on top as a mulch, it does not rob the root zone.

items.question: Which compound in dead plants takes the longest to break down?
options: Lignin, the tough compound in wood and bark
Simple sugars
Plant proteins
items.why: Microbes digest sugars and proteins in weeks and cellulose in months, whereas woody lignin takes years for fungi to break apart.

items.question: A year after you spread a barrow of compost on a bed, most of its volume has vanished. Where did it go?
options: Soil organisms ate it and breathed most of the carbon out as carbon dioxide
Rain washed it all deep underground into the water table
It weathered into sand and silt grains
items.why: Microbes and worms consume organic matter for energy and exhale the carbon as carbon dioxide gas, which is why beds need topping up every year.

items.question: How much compost should you add to an established bed each year, and how should you apply it?
options: Spread a 2 to 5 cm layer on the surface
Dig a thin dusting down to two spades' depth
Pile 30 cm on top every spring
items.why: A 2 to 5 cm layer replenishes what microbes eat each year, and spreading it on top lets worms pull it down without disturbing soil structure.

items.question: What is humus?
options: The dark, stable organic material left behind after plant remains have decayed
Fresh green plant clippings before they rot
A weathered mineral found in clay subsoils
items.why: Humus is the long-lasting organic fraction that remains after microbes and worms have digested fresh plant debris.

summary: **Organic matter feeds the soil, not just the plant.** Fertilizer feeds plants directly; organic matter feeds the life that supports them.
**It does several jobs at once.** It releases nutrients slowly, holds water, and supplies the glue that binds soil into crumbs.
**Balance browns and greens.** A heap rots fast near 25 to 30 parts carbon to 1 part nitrogen, kept damp and airy.
**Mulch woody material; do not dig it in.** Buried fresh wood ties up soil nitrogen for a while; spread on top, it does not.
**Top up every year.** Soil life eats most added organic matter within a couple of years, so add 2 to 5 cm of compost annually, on the surface.
**Compost safely.** Rot manure at least six months before using it on food beds, and keep meat, dairy and pet waste out of the heap.

humus.title: What humus really is
humus.text: **Humus** is the dark, long-lasting fraction of soil organic matter that remains after fresh plant debris has broken down. It holds several times its weight in water and carries negative electrical charges that hold onto plant nutrients (covered in Lesson 7). For decades, textbooks described humus as a collection of giant, virtually indestructible carbon molecules built during decay. Using modern microscopy and spectroscopy, soil scientists like Johannes Lehmann and Markus Kleber showed that most humus actually consists of smaller plant fragments and dead microbial cells—known as **necromass**—that survive for decades because they are chemically bonded to clay surfaces or sealed inside tiny soil crumbs where bacteria cannot reach them.

cn.title: Carbon-to-nitrogen ratio
cn.text: The **C:N ratio** compares the mass of carbon in a material to the mass of nitrogen. Fresh grass clippings sit around 15:1, kitchen scraps around 15:1 to 20:1, autumn leaves between 40:1 and 80:1, straw around 80:1, and wood chips at 400:1 or higher. Bacterial cells themselves have a C:N ratio near 5:1 to 8:1, but because microbes burn roughly two-thirds of the carbon they eat for energy and breathe it out as CO₂, they need a starting diet close to 25:1 or 30:1 to get the right balance.

heat.title: Why a compost heap gets hot
heat.text: A compost pile heats up purely from microbial respiration—the same chemical reaction as burning wood, just happening inside billions of cells at once. Once a pile is about a cubic metre in volume, the outer layers insulate the core and trap that heat. As the temperature climbs past 40 °C, everyday soil bacteria give way to heat-loving (**thermophilic**) bacteria and fungi that thrive up to 65 °C. Holding the core above 55 °C for three full days kills most weed seeds and plant pathogens, though a smaller, cool pile will still turn out good compost after a year or so.

robbery.title: Nitrogen immobilisation
robbery.text: When microbes pull dissolved ammonium (NH₄⁺) and nitrate (NO₃⁻) out of the soil to help them digest high-carbon materials like sawdust, soil scientists call it **nitrogen immobilisation**. The nitrogen is not lost from the bed; it is simply locked inside microbial proteins for a few weeks or months. Once the carbon runs low and those microbes die and get eaten by predators, the nitrogen returns to the soil in plant-available forms—a process called **mineralisation**.

herbicide.title: Persistent weedkillers in manure
herbicide.text: Certain broadleaf herbicides sprayed on pastures and hayfields—specifically **aminopyralid**, **clopyralid**, and **picloram**—pass straight through a horse or cow's digestive tract and remain active in the manure for a year or two. Even a few parts per billion in finished compost will severely curl and stunt sensitive crops like tomatoes, potatoes, peas, and beans. Before buying manure or hay, ask if the pasture was treated with persistent herbicides. You can also run a quick pot test at home: sow three pea or broad bean seeds in a pot mixed with the manure alongside a control pot of plain potting soil, and check after three weeks that the new leaves unfold flat rather than cupped and twisted.

model.title: Modelling decay rates
model.text: The diagram divides plant matter into three pools that decay at different speeds—sugars and proteins (half-life of about three weeks), cellulose and hemicellulose (half-life around five months), and woody lignin (half-life around four years)—while routing a small fraction of the digested carbon into long-term humus. Real decay rates in a garden depend heavily on temperature, moisture, and soil texture, so these curves illustrate the general pattern of decomposition rather than an exact timetable.
